claim: Testicular microcalcifications consist of hydroxyapatite.
source: Testicular microcalcifications consist of hydroxyapatite and have been associated with an increased risk of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs) but are also found in benign cases such as loss-of-function variants in the phosphate transporter SLC34A2.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work using Raman spectroscopy (De Jong et al., 2004; Smith et al., 1999) and confirmed by von Kossa and alizarin red staining in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications have been associated with an increased risk of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs).
source: Testicular microcalcifications consist of hydroxyapatite and have been associated with an increased risk of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs) but are also found in benign cases such as loss-of-function variants in the phosphate transporter SLC34A2.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Tan et al., 2010; Pedersen et al., 2016; Leblanc et al., 2018; Barbonetti et al., 2019).

claim: Testicular microcalcifications are found in benign cases such as loss-of-function variants in the phosphate transporter SLC34A2.
source: Testicular microcalcifications consist of hydroxyapatite and have been associated with an increased risk of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs) but are also found in benign cases such as loss-of-function variants in the phosphate transporter SLC34A2.
evidence: Supported by citation to Corut et al., 2006.

claim: FGF23 is expressed in testicular germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS).
source: Here, we show that fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a regulator of phosphate homeostasis, is expressed in testicular germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS), embryonal carcinoma (EC), and human embryonic stem cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining, qRT-PCR, and Western blot in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is expressed in embryonal carcinoma (EC).
source: Here, we show that fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a regulator of phosphate homeostasis, is expressed in testicular germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS), embryonal carcinoma (EC), and human embryonic stem cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining, qRT-PCR, Western blot, and seminal fluid measurements in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is expressed in human embryonic stem cells.
source: Here, we show that fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a regulator of phosphate homeostasis, is expressed in testicular germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS), embryonal carcinoma (EC), and human embryonic stem cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in hESC lines in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is not glycosylated in TGCTs.
source: FGF23 is not glycosylated in TGCTs and therefore cleaved into a C-terminal fragment which competitively antagonizes full-length FGF23.
evidence: Inferred from the detection of predominantly cFGF23 by Western blot and the absence of GalNAc-T3 expression in GCNIS and EC.

claim: FGF23 is cleaved into a C-terminal fragment in TGCTs which competitively antagonizes full-length FGF23.
source: FGF23 is not glycosylated in TGCTs and therefore cleaved into a C-terminal fragment which competitively antagonizes full-length FGF23.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot showing cFGF23 in GCNIS and EC, and supported by citation to Goetz et al., 2010 regarding competitive antagonism.

claim: Fgf23 knockout mice presented with marked calcifications in the epididymis.
source: Here, Fgf23 knockout mice presented with marked calcifications in the epididymis, spermatogenic arrest, and focally germ cells expressing the osteoblast marker Osteocalcin (gene name: Bglap, protein name).
evidence: Demonstrated by von Kossa and alizarin red staining in Fgf23-/- mice in the current study.

claim: Fgf23 knockout mice presented with spermatogenic arrest.
source: Here, Fgf23 knockout mice presented with marked calcifications in the epididymis, spermatogenic arrest, and focally germ cells expressing the osteoblast marker Osteocalcin (gene name: Bglap, protein name).
evidence: Observed in histological evaluation of Fgf23-/- mice in the current study.

claim: Fgf23 knockout mice have germ cells expressing the osteoblast marker Osteocalcin.
source: Here, Fgf23 knockout mice presented with marked calcifications in the epididymis, spermatogenic arrest, and focally germ cells expressing the osteoblast marker Osteocalcin (gene name: Bglap, protein name).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in Fgf23-/- mice in the current study.

claim: Mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins have frequent testicular microcalcifications.
source: Moreover, the frequent testicular microcalcifications in mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins are associated with lower Slc34a2 and higher Bglap/Slc34a1 (protein name: NPT2a) expression compared with wild-type mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by von Kossa and alizarin red staining in hpg.ARKO mice in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications in mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins are associated with lower Slc34a2 expression compared with wild-type mice.
source: Moreover, the frequent testicular microcalcifications in mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins are associated with lower Slc34a2 and higher Bglap/Slc34a1 (protein name: NPT2a) expression compared with wild-type mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in hpg.ARKO mice in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications in mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins are associated with higher Slc34a1 expression compared with wild-type mice.
source: Moreover, the frequent testicular microcalcifications in mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins are associated with lower Slc34a2 and higher Bglap/Slc34a1 (protein name: NPT2a) expression compared with wild-type mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in hpg.ARKO mice in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications in mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins are associated with higher Bglap expression compared with wild-type mice.
source: Moreover, the frequent testicular microcalcifications in mice with no functional androgen receptor and lack of circulating gonadotropins are associated with lower Slc34a2 and higher Bglap/Slc34a1 (protein name: NPT2a) expression compared with wild-type mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in hpg.ARKO mice in the current study.

claim: Human testicular specimens with microcalcifications have lower SLC34A2 expression.
source: In accordance, human testicular specimens with microcalcifications also have lower SLC34A2 and a subpopulation of germ cells express phosphate transporter NPT2a, Osteocalcin, and RUNX2 highlighting aberrant local phosphate handling and expression of bone-specific proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in human testicular specimens with GCNIS in the current study.

claim: A subpopulation of germ cells in human testicular specimens with microcalcifications express phosphate transporter NPT2a.
source: In accordance, human testicular specimens with microcalcifications also have lower SLC34A2 and a subpopulation of germ cells express phosphate transporter NPT2a, Osteocalcin, and RUNX2 highlighting aberrant local phosphate handling and expression of bone-specific proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens with microcalcifications in the current study.

claim: A subpopulation of germ cells in human testicular specimens with microcalcifications express Osteocalcin.
source: In accordance, human testicular specimens with microcalcifications also have lower SLC34A2 and a subpopulation of germ cells express phosphate transporter NPT2a, Osteocalcin, and RUNX2 highlighting aberrant local phosphate handling and expression of bone-specific proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens with microcalcifications in the current study.

claim: A subpopulation of germ cells in human testicular specimens with microcalcifications express RUNX2.
source: In accordance, human testicular specimens with microcalcifications also have lower SLC34A2 and a subpopulation of germ cells express phosphate transporter NPT2a, Osteocalcin, and RUNX2 highlighting aberrant local phosphate handling and expression of bone-specific proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens with microcalcifications in the current study.

claim: Calcium or phosphate treatment induced deposition of calcium phosphate in a spermatogonial cell line.
source: Mineral disturbance in vitro using calcium or phosphate treatment induced deposition of calcium phosphate in a spermatogonial cell line and this effect was fully rescued by the mineralization inhibitor pyrophosphate.
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells treated with calcium and/or phosphate in the current study.

claim: The mineralization induced by calcium or phosphate in a spermatogonial cell line was fully rescued by the mineralization inhibitor pyrophosphate.
source: Mineral disturbance in vitro using calcium or phosphate treatment induced deposition of calcium phosphate in a spermatogonial cell line and this effect was fully rescued by the mineralization inhibitor pyrophosphate.
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells treated with calcium, phosphate, and pyrophosphate in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications arise secondary to local alterations in mineral homeostasis.
source: In conclusion, testicular microcalcifications arise secondary to local alterations in mineral homeostasis, which in combination with impaired Sertoli cell function and reduced levels of mineralization inhibitors due to high alkaline phosphatase activity in GCNIS and TGCTs facilitate osteogenic-like differentiation of testicular cells and deposition of hydroxyapatite.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including altered phosphate transporter expression, effects of mineral treatments in vitro, and observations in multiple mouse models.

claim: Impaired Sertoli cell function facilitates testicular microcalcifications.
source: In conclusion, testicular microcalcifications arise secondary to local alterations in mineral homeostasis, which in combination with impaired Sertoli cell function and reduced levels of mineralization inhibitors due to high alkaline phosphatase activity in GCNIS and TGCTs facilitate osteogenic-like differentiation of testicular cells and deposition of hydroxyapatite.
evidence: Demonstrated by observations in hpg, hpg.SCARKO, hpg.ARKO mice, and Sertoli cell-ablated mice in the current study.

claim: High alkaline phosphatase activity in GCNIS and TGCTs reduces levels of mineralization inhibitors.
source: In conclusion, testicular microcalcifications arise secondary to local alterations in mineral homeostasis, which in combination with impaired Sertoli cell function and reduced levels of mineralization inhibitors due to high alkaline phosphatase activity in GCNIS and TGCTs facilitate osteogenic-like differentiation of testicular cells and deposition of hydroxyapatite.
evidence: Demonstrated by NBT/BCIP staining showing high ALP activity in GCNIS, and supported by the effect of pyrophosphate in preventing mineralization in GC1 cells.

claim: Osteogenic-like differentiation of testicular cells facilitates deposition of hydroxyapatite.
source: In conclusion, testicular microcalcifications arise secondary to local alterations in mineral homeostasis, which in combination with impaired Sertoli cell function and reduced levels of mineralization inhibitors due to high alkaline phosphatase activity in GCNIS and TGCTs facilitate osteogenic-like differentiation of testicular cells and deposition of hydroxyapatite.
evidence: Demonstrated by expression of bone markers (Osteocalcin, RUNX2, DMP1, OPN) in testicular cells adjacent to microcalcifications in both human and mouse specimens.

claim: Testicular microlithiasis in infertile men is associated with an increased risk of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs).
source: Testicular microlithiasis in infertile men is associated with an increased risk of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs) (Tan et al., 2010; Pedersen et al., 2016; Leblanc et al., 2018; Barbonetti et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Tan et al., 2010; Pedersen et al., 2016; Leblanc et al., 2018; Barbonetti et al., 2019).

claim: Ultrasonic and histological microcalcifications are frequent findings in the testis of asymptomatic men.
source: However, both ultrasonic and histological microcalcifications are also frequent findings in the testis of asymptomatic men and the etiology remains largely unknown in both malignant and benign cases.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Histological microcalcifications consist of hydroxyapatite as shown by Raman spectroscopy.
source: The histological microcalcifications have been shown by Raman spectroscopy to consist of hydroxyapatite (De Jong et al., 2004; Smith et al., 1999), which is normally found exclusively in the skeleton and requires the presence of cells with osteoblast-like characteristics (Kirsch, 2006; Boström et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies using Raman spectroscopy (De Jong et al., 2004; Smith et al., 1999).

claim: Hydroxyapatite is normally found exclusively in the skeleton.
source: The histological microcalcifications have been shown by Raman spectroscopy to consist of hydroxyapatite (De Jong et al., 2004; Smith et al., 1999), which is normally found exclusively in the skeleton and requires the presence of cells with osteoblast-like characteristics (Kirsch, 2006; Boström et al., 1995).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and supported by citations (Kirsch, 2006; Boström et al., 1995).

claim: Hydroxyapatite formation requires the presence of cells with osteoblast-like characteristics.
source: The histological microcalcifications have been shown by Raman spectroscopy to consist of hydroxyapatite (De Jong et al., 2004; Smith et al., 1999), which is normally found exclusively in the skeleton and requires the presence of cells with osteoblast-like characteristics (Kirsch, 2006; Boström et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kirsch, 2006; Boström et al., 1995).

claim: Extra-skeletal mineralization is often caused by an imbalance in promoters and inhibitors of biomineralization.
source: Extra-skeletal mineralization is often caused by an imbalance in promoters and inhibitors of biomineralization (Kirsch, 2006; Rowe, 2012; Martin and Quarles, 2012; Shanahan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kirsch, 2006; Rowe, 2012; Martin and Quarles, 2012; Shanahan et al., 2011).

claim: Tissue mineralization is tightly controlled by small integrin-binding ligand N-linked glycoproteins (SIBLINGs) such as osteopontin (OPN) and dentin matrix acidic phosphoprotein 1 (DMP1).
source: Tissue mineralization is tightly controlled by small integrin-binding ligand N-linked glycoproteins (SIBLINGs) such as osteopontin (OPN) and dentin matrix acidic phosphoprotein 1 (DMP1) that regulate mineralization in concert with osteocalcin and runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pyrophosphate (PPi) generated by ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1) is an essential suppressor of hydroxyapatite deposition.
source: Pyrophosphate (PPi) generated by ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1) is an essential suppressor of hydroxyapatite deposition and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) inactivates PPi (Hessle et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hessle et al., 2002.

claim: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) inactivates pyrophosphate (PPi).
source: Pyrophosphate (PPi) generated by ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1) is an essential suppressor of hydroxyapatite deposition and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) inactivates PPi (Hessle et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hessle et al., 2002.

claim: ALP abundance is a central factor for local phosphate homeostasis.
source: ALP abundance is thus a central factor for local phosphate homeostasis, and during osteogenic differentiation increased ALP activity is a hallmark of the bone-like characteristics of the cells in other extra-skeletal tissue such as blood vessels.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and supported by the role of ALP in inactivating PPi.

claim: During osteogenic differentiation increased ALP activity is a hallmark of the bone-like characteristics of cells in extra-skeletal tissue such as blood vessels.
source: ALP abundance is thus a central factor for local phosphate homeostasis, and during osteogenic differentiation increased ALP activity is a hallmark of the bone-like characteristics of the cells in other extra-skeletal tissue such as blood vessels.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: All four isozymes of ALP can be found in TGCTs.
source: In this paper, ALP is used as an acronym for all four isozymes of ALP as all can be found in TGCTs (Hofmann et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hofmann et al., 1989.

claim: FGF23, Klotho, phosphate transport proteins NPT2-a and -b, and vitamin D metabolizing enzymes are essential for maintaining stable mineral homeostasis.
source: In addition, accumulating evidence suggests that fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) and its receptor Klotho (gene name: KL), the phosphate transport proteins solute carrier family NPT2-a and -b (gene names: SLC34A-1 and -2, respectively), and vitamin D metabolizing enzymes are essential for maintaining stable mineral homeostasis and that imbalance in their activity may lead to extra-skeletal calcifications (Yuan et al., 2014; Lieben et al., 2012; Golub, 2009; Komori et al., 1997; Ducy et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Yuan et al., 2014; Lieben et al., 2012; Golub, 2009; Komori et al., 1997; Ducy et al., 1996).

claim: Imbalance in the activity of FGF23, Klotho, phosphate transport proteins, and vitamin D metabolizing enzymes may lead to extra-skeletal calcifications.
source: In addition, accumulating evidence suggests that fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) and its receptor Klotho (gene name: KL), the phosphate transport proteins solute carrier family NPT2-a and -b (gene names: SLC34A-1 and -2, respectively), and vitamin D metabolizing enzymes are essential for maintaining stable mineral homeostasis and that imbalance in their activity may lead to extra-skeletal calcifications (Yuan et al., 2014; Lieben et al., 2012; Golub, 2009; Komori et al., 1997; Ducy et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Yuan et al., 2014; Lieben et al., 2012; Golub, 2009; Komori et al., 1997; Ducy et al., 1996).

claim: Loss-of-function variants in the GALNT3 gene lead to a lack of degradation-protective glycosylation of FGF23.
source: Interestingly, loss-of-function variants in the GALNT3 gene (protein name: GalNAc-T3) and hence a lack of degradation-protective glycosylation of FGF23 leads to systemic hyperphosphatemia and severe testicular microcalcifications (Garringer et al., 2007; Campagnoli et al., 2006; Kato et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Garringer et al., 2007; Campagnoli et al., 2006; Kato et al., 2006).

claim: Loss-of-function variants in the GALNT3 gene lead to systemic hyperphosphatemia and severe testicular microcalcifications.
source: Interestingly, loss-of-function variants in the GALNT3 gene (protein name: GalNAc-T3) and hence a lack of degradation-protective glycosylation of FGF23 leads to systemic hyperphosphatemia and severe testicular microcalcifications (Garringer et al., 2007; Campagnoli et al., 2006; Kato et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Garringer et al., 2007; Campagnoli et al., 2006; Kato et al., 2006).

claim: Intratesticular phosphate levels are essential in the formation of testicular microlithiasis.
source: Intratesticular phosphate levels seem to be essential in the formation of testicular microlithiasis as loss-of-function variants in the main testicular phosphate transporter SLC34A2 also lead to severe testicular microcalcifications without affecting systemic phosphate levels (Corut et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corut et al., 2006 showing that loss-of-function in SLC34A2 causes testicular microcalcifications without affecting systemic phosphate.

claim: Loss-of-function variants in the main testicular phosphate transporter SLC34A2 lead to severe testicular microcalcifications without affecting systemic phosphate levels.
source: Intratesticular phosphate levels seem to be essential in the formation of testicular microlithiasis as loss-of-function variants in the main testicular phosphate transporter SLC34A2 also lead to severe testicular microcalcifications without affecting systemic phosphate levels (Corut et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corut et al., 2006.

claim: Testicular microlithiasis is found in patients with loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding ABCC6.
source: Testicular microlithiasis is also found in patients with loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding ATP binding cassette subfamily C member 6 (ABCC6), which results in abnormal PPi metabolism and thus less inhibition of mineralization (Vanakker et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanakker et al., 2006.

claim: Loss-of-function variants in ABCC6 result in abnormal PPi metabolism and less inhibition of mineralization.
source: Testicular microlithiasis is also found in patients with loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding ATP binding cassette subfamily C member 6 (ABCC6), which results in abnormal PPi metabolism and thus less inhibition of mineralization (Vanakker et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanakker et al., 2006.

claim: Local and systemic changes in phosphate homeostasis induce testicular microcalcifications.
source: These studies show that particularly local and potentially systemic changes in phosphate homeostasis induce testicular microcalcifications.
evidence: Inferred from the cited studies showing that loss-of-function in SLC34A2, GALNT3, and ABCC6 lead to testicular microcalcifications.

claim: TGCTs originate from a common progenitor germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS).
source: TGCTs originate from a common progenitor germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS), which is characterized by the expression of pluripotency factors such as octamer-binding transcription factor 4 (gene names: POU5F1, protein name: OCT4), NANOG, and high ALP activity (Hofmann et al., 1989; Skakkebaek, 1972; Rajpert-De Meyts et al., 2004; Hart et al., 2005; Jacobsen and Nørgaard‐pedersen, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hofmann et al., 1989; Skakkebaek, 1972; Rajpert-De Meyts et al., 2004; Hart et al., 2005; Jacobsen and Nørgaard‐pedersen, 1984).

claim: GCNIS is characterized by the expression of pluripotency factors such as OCT4, NANOG, and high ALP activity.
source: TGCTs originate from a common progenitor germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS), which is characterized by the expression of pluripotency factors such as octamer-binding transcription factor 4 (gene names: POU5F1, protein name: OCT4), NANOG, and high ALP activity (Hofmann et al., 1989; Skakkebaek, 1972; Rajpert-De Meyts et al., 2004; Hart et al., 2005; Jacobsen and Nørgaard‐pedersen, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hofmann et al., 1989; Skakkebaek, 1972; Rajpert-De Meyts et al., 2004; Hart et al., 2005; Jacobsen and Nørgaard‐pedersen, 1984).

claim: GCNIS cells undergo malignant transformation and form either a seminoma or a non-seminoma.
source: GCNIS cells undergo malignant transformation and form either a seminoma that retains germ cell characteristics or a non-seminoma that may contain embryonal carcinoma (EC) resembling human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), teratoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, or a combination of these (Rodriguez et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2003.

claim: Duplication of chromosome 12p is the most consistent chromosomal aberration during the malignant transformation of GCNIS into invasive TGCTs.
source: During the malignant transformation of GCNIS into invasive TGCTs, duplication of chromosome 12p (often as isochromosome 12p) is the most consistent chromosomal aberration and may be involved in the dedifferentiation from GCNIS to EC (Rodriguez et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2003.

claim: Duplication of chromosome 12p may be involved in the dedifferentiation from GCNIS to EC.
source: During the malignant transformation of GCNIS into invasive TGCTs, duplication of chromosome 12p (often as isochromosome 12p) is the most consistent chromosomal aberration and may be involved in the dedifferentiation from GCNIS to EC (Rodriguez et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2003 and speculation about the role of chromosome 12p duplication.

claim: In healthy individuals, FGF23 is produced exclusively in osteocytes.
source: In healthy individuals, FGF23 is produced exclusively in osteocytes, and the location of the gene on chromosome 12p may be important for its presence and role in TGCTs.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The FGF23 gene is located on chromosome 12p.
source: In healthy individuals, FGF23 is produced exclusively in osteocytes, and the location of the gene on chromosome 12p may be important for its presence and role in TGCTs.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: The location of the FGF23 gene on chromosome 12p may be important for its presence and role in TGCTs.
source: In healthy individuals, FGF23 is produced exclusively in osteocytes, and the location of the gene on chromosome 12p may be important for its presence and role in TGCTs.
evidence: Speculated based on the duplication of chromosome 12p in TGCTs and the observed expression of FGF23 in TGCTs.

claim: Full-length FGF23 increases phosphate excretion by decreasing the luminal expression of NPT2a in the kidney.
source: Full-length FGF23 increases phosphate excretion by decreasing the luminal expression of NPT2a in the kidney and by lowering the concentration of active vitamin D via increased expression of the inactivating enzyme CYP24A1 and reduced expression of the activating enzyme CYP27B1 (Shimada et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shimada et al., 2004.

claim: Full-length FGF23 lowers the concentration of active vitamin D via increased expression of CYP24A1 and reduced expression of CYP27B1.
source: Full-length FGF23 increases phosphate excretion by decreasing the luminal expression of NPT2a in the kidney and by lowering the concentration of active vitamin D via increased expression of the inactivating enzyme CYP24A1 and reduced expression of the activating enzyme CYP27B1 (Shimada et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shimada et al., 2004.

claim: The local metabolism of vitamin D disappeared during the malignant transformation of GCNIS to EC.
source: We have previously shown that the local metabolism of vitamin D disappeared during the malignant transformation of GCNIS to EC and that FGF23 was expressed in an EC-derived cell line (Blomberg Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Blomberg Jensen et al., 2012).

claim: FGF23 is expressed in an EC-derived cell line.
source: We have previously shown that the local metabolism of vitamin D disappeared during the malignant transformation of GCNIS to EC and that FGF23 was expressed in an EC-derived cell line (Blomberg Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Blomberg Jensen et al., 2012).

claim: O-glycosylation by GalNAc-T3 protects FGF23 from rapid degradation.
source: O-glycosylation by GalNAc-T3 protects FGF23 from rapid degradation, and full-length FGF23 activates a receptor complex consisting of Klotho heterodimerization with FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Full-length FGF23 activates a receptor complex consisting of Klotho heterodimerization with FGFR1.
source: O-glycosylation by GalNAc-T3 protects FGF23 from rapid degradation, and full-length FGF23 activates a receptor complex consisting of Klotho heterodimerization with FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cleaved C-terminal fragment of FGF23 can bind and serve as a competitive antagonist for intact FGF23.
source: However, the cleaved C-terminal fragment (cFGF23) can bind and serve as a competitive antagonist for intact FGF23 (iFGF23), and iFGF23 can also induce Klotho-independent effects (Goetz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goetz et al., 2010.

claim: Intact FGF23 can induce Klotho-independent effects.
source: However, the cleaved C-terminal fragment (cFGF23) can bind and serve as a competitive antagonist for intact FGF23 (iFGF23), and iFGF23 can also induce Klotho-independent effects (Goetz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goetz et al., 2010.

claim: Loss-of-function variants in FGF23, GALNT3, or KL lead to tumoral calcinosis partly through osteogenic-like differentiation of mesenchymal-derived cells.
source: Loss-of-function variants in the genes FGF23, GALNT3, or KL lead to tumoral calcinosis partly through osteogenic-like differentiation of mesenchymal-derived cells due to altered mineral homeostasis and vitamin D metabolism (Farrow et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farrow et al., 2011.

claim: The renal phosphate transporter NPT2a is ectopically expressed in GCNIS-containing tubules adjacent to microcalcifications.
source: In GCNIS-containing tubules adjacent to microcalcifications, we found that the renal phosphate transporter NPT2a and FGF23 were ectopically expressed.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is ectopically expressed in GCNIS-containing tubules adjacent to microcalcifications.
source: In GCNIS-containing tubules adjacent to microcalcifications, we found that the renal phosphate transporter NPT2a and FGF23 were ectopically expressed.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: Klotho is expressed in the cytoplasm of germ cells in normal tubules.
source: In contrast, Klotho was expressed in the cytoplasm of the germ cells in normal tubules, with or without adjacent microcalcifications, but not in GCNIS.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: Klotho is not expressed in GCNIS.
source: In contrast, Klotho was expressed in the cytoplasm of the germ cells in normal tubules, with or without adjacent microcalcifications, but not in GCNIS.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: FGFR1 expression is found in both GCNIS and normal tubules.
source: FGFR1 expression was found in both GCNIS and normal tubules (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: Osteocalcin is expressed in tissue with GCNIS and adjacent to microcalcifications but not in normal tubules with full spermatogenesis.
source: The expression of the bone marker Osteocalcin was present in tissue with GCNIS and adjacent to the microcalcifications but not the normal tubules with full spermatogenesis (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications vary in size from small calcifications focally in the center of seminiferous tubules to occupying most of the intraluminal area.
source: The microcalcifications vary in size from small calcifications focally in the center of seminiferous tubules to occupying most of the intraluminal area (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by von Kossa staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: In sporadic severe cases there is intratesticular bone formation.
source: In sporadic severe cases there was intratesticular bone formation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological examination and RUNX2 staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: RUNX2 is not expressed in testes with normal spermatogenesis.
source: The early osteoblast marker RUNX2 was not expressed in testes with normal spermatogenesis.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: When microcalcifications or bone formation are detected, a small fraction of germ cells occasionally have cytoplasmic staining of RUNX2.
source: However, occasionally, when microcalcifications or bone formation were detected, a small fraction of the germ cells in the seminiferous tubules had cytoplasmic staining of RUNX2 supporting a bone-like phenotype of some germ cells (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: SLC34A1 is expressed at a very low level in normal testis but is highly expressed in 25% of specimens containing GCNIS.
source: SLC34A1 was expressed at a very low level in normal testis but was highly expressed in 25% of the specimens containing GCNIS.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: The phosphate transporter SLC34A2 is abundantly expressed in germ cells from normal testis but the expression is lower in specimens containing GCNIS.
source: In contrast, the phosphate transporter SLC34A2 was abundantly expressed in the germ cells from normal testis but the expression was lower in specimens containing GCNIS (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: The transcriptional level of FGF23 is highest in EC components and significantly higher compared with normal testis.
source: The transcriptional level of FGF23 was highest in EC components, significantly higher compared with normal testis, and was positively correlated with the expression of the pluripotency factor NANOG but not significantly with POU5F1 (r=0.813, p=0.049, and r=0.780, p=0.068, respectively).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: FGF23 expression is positively correlated with the expression of NANOG in EC.
source: The transcriptional level of FGF23 was highest in EC components, significantly higher compared with normal testis, and was positively correlated with the expression of the pluripotency factor NANOG but not significantly with POU5F1 (r=0.813, p=0.049, and r=0.780, p=0.068, respectively).
evidence: Demonstrated by Pearson correlation analysis of qRT-PCR data in the current study.

claim: Two EC specimens with polyembryoma components had several fold higher levels of FGF23.
source: Two EC specimens with polyembryoma components (the most dedifferentiated structure resembling early embryonic formation) had several fold higher levels of FGF23 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: A higher expression of FGF23 in GCNIS compared with normal testis was confirmed in microdissected GCNIS cells.
source: A higher expression of FGF23 in GCNIS compared with normal testis was also confirmed in microdissected GCNIS cells, while fetal gonocytes and hESCs also expressed FGF23 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray analysis of microdissected cells in the current study.

claim: Fetal gonocytes express FGF23.
source: A higher expression of FGF23 in GCNIS compared with normal testis was also confirmed in microdissected GCNIS cells, while fetal gonocytes and hESCs also expressed FGF23 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray analysis in the current study.

claim: hESCs express FGF23.
source: A higher expression of FGF23 in GCNIS compared with normal testis was also confirmed in microdissected GCNIS cells, while fetal gonocytes and hESCs also expressed FGF23 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray analysis and qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: hESC cells and the EC-derived cell line NTera2 have ~30-fold higher expression of FGF23 compared with normal testis.
source: The high expression of FGF23 in hESC and EC was validated by a ~30-fold higher expression in different strains of hESC cells and the EC-derived cell line NTera2 compared with normal testis (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: Normal testicular tissue has high expression of the FGF23 receptor Klotho.
source: In contrast, normal testicular tissue had a high expression of the FGF23 receptor Klotho (KL), whereas the expression was low in GCNIS cells and hESC (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray analysis in the current study.

claim: Klotho expression is low in GCNIS cells and hESC.
source: In contrast, normal testicular tissue had a high expression of the FGF23 receptor Klotho (KL), whereas the expression was low in GCNIS cells and hESC (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray analysis in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is expressed solely in OCT4-positive GCNIS cells.
source: IHC confirmed the marked expression of FGF23 solely in OCT4-positive GCNIS cells that also expressed FGFR1, while Klotho was exclusively expressed in normal germ cells and not found in any of the OCT4-positive cancer cells including seminoma and EC (Figure 2E and Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: GCNIS cells express FGFR1.
source: IHC confirmed the marked expression of FGF23 solely in OCT4-positive GCNIS cells that also expressed FGFR1, while Klotho was exclusively expressed in normal germ cells and not found in any of the OCT4-positive cancer cells including seminoma and EC (Figure 2E and Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: Klotho is exclusively expressed in normal germ cells and not found in any OCT4-positive cancer cells including seminoma and EC.
source: IHC confirmed the marked expression of FGF23 solely in OCT4-positive GCNIS cells that also expressed FGFR1, while Klotho was exclusively expressed in normal germ cells and not found in any of the OCT4-positive cancer cells including seminoma and EC (Figure 2E and Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is expressed in EC cells characterized by concomitant OCT4 expression.
source: FGF23 was also expressed in the EC cells characterized by concomitant OCT4 expression but was virtually absent in seminoma cells despite their marked OCT4 expression suggesting that the chromosome 12p duplication (occurring in both seminoma and EC) alone is not sufficient to maintain FGF23 production.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is virtually absent in seminoma cells despite their marked OCT4 expression.
source: FGF23 was also expressed in the EC cells characterized by concomitant OCT4 expression but was virtually absent in seminoma cells despite their marked OCT4 expression suggesting that the chromosome 12p duplication (occurring in both seminoma and EC) alone is not sufficient to maintain FGF23 production.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: Chromosome 12p duplication alone is not sufficient to maintain FGF23 production.
source: FGF23 was also expressed in the EC cells characterized by concomitant OCT4 expression but was virtually absent in seminoma cells despite their marked OCT4 expression suggesting that the chromosome 12p duplication (occurring in both seminoma and EC) alone is not sufficient to maintain FGF23 production.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that seminoma has chromosome 12p duplication but does not express FGF23, while EC has both and does express FGF23.

claim: Western blot confirmed the presence of FGF23 with two bands corresponding to the sizes of cFGF23 and iFGF23 in GCNIS and EC.
source: Western blot confirmed the presence of FGF23 with two bands corresponding to the sizes of cFGF23 and iFGF23 in GCNIS and EC.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in human testicular specimens in the current study.

claim: cFGF23 is expressed in NTera2 cells.
source: cFGF23 was also expressed in NTera2 cells, and neither cFGF23 nor iFGF23 were detected in normal testis or the seminoma-derived cell line TCam2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in the current study.

claim: Neither cFGF23 nor iFGF23 are detected in normal testis or the seminoma-derived cell line TCam2.
source: cFGF23 was also expressed in NTera2 cells, and neither cFGF23 nor iFGF23 were detected in normal testis or the seminoma-derived cell line TCam2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in the current study.

claim: cFGF23 and iFGF23 are expressed in an anaplastic seminoma sample.
source: cFGF23 and iFGF23 were expressed in an anaplastic seminoma sample, which is considered a rare intermediate between seminoma and EC due to the high proliferative index and morphological resemblance with EC (Figure 2F and Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in the current study.

claim: Healthy men have undetectable iFGF23 levels in seminal fluid.
source: Healthy men had undetectable iFGF23 levels in the seminal fluid, and a few (8/19) men had detectable cFGF23.
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA measurements in seminal fluid in the current study.

claim: A few men with GCNIS or EC have detectable levels of iFGF23 in seminal fluid.
source: A few men with GCNIS (2/7) or EC (2/10) had detectable levels of iFGF23 in the seminal fluid whereas total FGF23 were detected in the majority (9/10) of men with EC and their total FGF23 concentration in seminal fluid was significantly higher compared with healthy men (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA measurements in seminal fluid in the current study.

claim: Total FGF23 is detected in the majority of men with EC.
source: A few men with GCNIS (2/7) or EC (2/10) had detectable levels of iFGF23 in the seminal fluid whereas total FGF23 were detected in the majority (9/10) of men with EC and their total FGF23 concentration in seminal fluid was significantly higher compared with healthy men (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA measurements in seminal fluid in the current study.

claim: Total FGF23 concentration in seminal fluid is significantly higher in men with EC compared with healthy men.
source: A few men with GCNIS (2/7) or EC (2/10) had detectable levels of iFGF23 in the seminal fluid whereas total FGF23 were detected in the majority (9/10) of men with EC and their total FGF23 concentration in seminal fluid was significantly higher compared with healthy men (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA measurements and statistical analysis in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is expressed in only 5-10% of NTera2 xenograft tumor cells.
source: In NTera2 xenograft tumors, FGF23 was expressed in only 5–10% of tumor cells, which shows that the phenotype of the NTera2 cells changes in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in NTera2 xenograft tumors in the current study.

claim: The phenotype of NTera2 cells changes in vivo.
source: In NTera2 xenograft tumors, FGF23 was expressed in only 5–10% of tumor cells, which shows that the phenotype of the NTera2 cells changes in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FGF23 is expressed in only 5-10% of tumor cells in vivo compared to in vitro.

claim: Human iFGF23 in serum from nude mice with NTera2 tumors is fourfold higher compared with control nude mice.
source: Human iFGF23 in serum from nude mice with tumors was fourfold higher compared with control nude mice (Figure 3B) and thus much lower than the EC tumor samples.
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA measurements in mouse serum in the current study.

claim: The presence of iFGF23 in serum and undetectable levels in NTera2 cells grown in vitro suggests that NTera2 cells xenografted into nude mice undergo somatic differentiation in response to host stimuli.
source: The presence of iFGF23 in serum and the undetectable levels of iFGF23 in NTera2 cells grown in vitro suggests that NTera2 cells xenografted into nude mice undergo somatic differentiation in response to host stimuli and facilitate GalNAc-T3-mediated glycosylation of iFGF23 to prevent its cleavage (Figure 2F).
evidence: Inferred from the detection of iFGF23 in serum of xenografted mice but not in NTera2 cells in vitro.

claim: NTera2 tumor-bearing mice have significantly higher Slc34a1 and Bglap expression in testis compared with nude mice without tumors.
source: Interestingly, NTera2 tumor-bearing mice had significantly higher Slc34a1 and bone gamma-carboxyglutamic acid-containing protein (Bglap) expression in testis compared with nude mice without tumors but no change in Slc34a2, suggesting that the effect induced by the tumor was cFGF23 or FGF23 independent (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in mouse testis in the current study.

claim: NTera2 tumor-bearing mice have no change in Slc34a2 expression in testis compared with nude mice without tumors.
source: Interestingly, NTera2 tumor-bearing mice had significantly higher Slc34a1 and bone gamma-carboxyglutamic acid-containing protein (Bglap) expression in testis compared with nude mice without tumors but no change in Slc34a2, suggesting that the effect induced by the tumor was cFGF23 or FGF23 independent (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in mouse testis in the current study.

claim: The effect on testicular gene expression induced by NTera2 tumors is cFGF23 or FGF23 independent.
source: Interestingly, NTera2 tumor-bearing mice had significantly higher Slc34a1 and bone gamma-carboxyglutamic acid-containing protein (Bglap) expression in testis compared with nude mice without tumors but no change in Slc34a2, suggesting that the effect induced by the tumor was cFGF23 or FGF23 independent (Figure 3C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the tumor induces changes in testicular gene expression despite low levels of FGF23, and supported by the ex vivo experiment showing no effect of exogenous FGF23.

claim: Exogenous treatment with iFGF23 or cFGF23 in human testis specimens cultured ex vivo for 24 hr does not change the expression of phosphate transporters or BGLAP.
source: Exogenous treatment with iFGF23 or cFGF23 in human testis specimens cultured ex vivo for 24 hr did not change the expression of phosphate transporters or BGLAP (Figure 3D), indicating that FGF23 alone is not responsible for the change in expression of these genes but may be caused by other factors released or induced by the tumors.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in human testis ex vivo cultures in the current study.

claim: FGF23 alone is not responsible for the change in expression of phosphate transporters and BGLAP but may be caused by other factors released or induced by tumors.
source: Exogenous treatment with iFGF23 or cFGF23 in human testis specimens cultured ex vivo for 24 hr did not change the expression of phosphate transporters or BGLAP (Figure 3D), indicating that FGF23 alone is not responsible for the change in expression of these genes but may be caused by other factors released or induced by the tumors.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of exogenous FGF23 treatment in ex vivo cultures.

claim: Fgf23-/- mice have elevated serum concentrations of calcium and phosphate.
source: Fgf23-/- mice had elevated serum concentrations of calcium and phosphate, smaller testes, and often spermatogenic arrest at the spermatocyte stage compared with control mice (Figure 4A and data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by biochemical measurements in mouse serum in the current study.

claim: Fgf23-/- mice have smaller testes compared with control mice.
source: Fgf23-/- mice had elevated serum concentrations of calcium and phosphate, smaller testes, and often spermatogenic arrest at the spermatocyte stage compared with control mice (Figure 4A and data not shown).
evidence: Observed in the current study.

claim: Fgf23-/- mice often have spermatogenic arrest at the spermatocyte stage.
source: Fgf23-/- mice had elevated serum concentrations of calcium and phosphate, smaller testes, and often spermatogenic arrest at the spermatocyte stage compared with control mice (Figure 4A and data not shown).
evidence: Observed in histological evaluation in the current study.

claim: Testicular evaluation of Fgf23-/- mice showed no deposition of hydroxyapatite.
source: Testicular evaluation showed no deposition of hydroxyapatite, but DMP1, OPN, and Osteocalcin were expressed in the cytoplasm of some germ cells in up to 15% of the tubules in Fgf23-/- mice and more rarely in WT mice (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by von Kossa and alizarin red staining in the current study.

claim: DMP1, OPN, and Osteocalcin are expressed in the cytoplasm of some germ cells in up to 15% of tubules in Fgf23-/- mice.
source: Testicular evaluation showed no deposition of hydroxyapatite, but DMP1, OPN, and Osteocalcin were expressed in the cytoplasm of some germ cells in up to 15% of the tubules in Fgf23-/- mice and more rarely in WT mice (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in the current study.

claim: Short-term high serum phosphate does not induce testicular microlithiasis in WT mice.
source: To distinguish the effects of FGF23 loss from high phosphate alone, WT mice received a high phosphate diet, which showed that short-term high serum phosphate did not induce testicular microlithiasis or induce any testicular changes in the expression of phosphate transporters or Bgalp (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by von Kossa/alizarin red staining and qRT-PCR in mice fed high phosphate diet in the current study.

claim: Short-term high serum phosphate does not induce testicular changes in the expression of phosphate transporters or Bglap in WT mice.
source: To distinguish the effects of FGF23 loss from high phosphate alone, WT mice received a high phosphate diet, which showed that short-term high serum phosphate did not induce testicular microlithiasis or induce any testicular changes in the expression of phosphate transporters or Bgalp (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in mice fed high phosphate diet in the current study.

claim: Marked mineralization is observed in cauda epididymis in 25% of Fgf23-/- mice and none of the WT mice.
source: A more severe phenotype was observed in cauda epididymis with marked mineralization in 25% of the Fgf23-/- mice and none of the WT mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by von Kossa and alizarin red staining in the current study.

claim: DMP1, OPN, and Osteocalcin are highly expressed in the epididymis of Fgf23-/- mice.
source: DMP1, OPN, and Osteocalcin were highly expressed in the epididymis of Fgf23-/- mice (Figure 4E and F), while DMP1 and Osteocalcin were not detected in the epididymal lumen of WT mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in the current study.

claim: DMP1 and Osteocalcin are not detected in the epididymal lumen of WT mice.
source: DMP1, OPN, and Osteocalcin were highly expressed in the epididymis of Fgf23-/- mice (Figure 4E and F), while DMP1 and Osteocalcin were not detected in the epididymal lumen of WT mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in the current study.

claim: OPN is expressed in the head of sperm in both WT and Fgf23-/- mice.
source: OPN was expressed in the head of sperm in both WT and Fgf23-/- mice, although it was expressed exclusively in the luminal part in the calcified section of the epididymis of Fgf23-/- mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications are found in ~30% of hypogonadal (hpg) mice that lack circulating gonadotropins.
source: Testicular microcalcifications are not exclusively found in mice with knockout of phosphate transport regulators but also in ~30% of hypogonadal (hpg) mice that lack circulating gonadotropins (follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone).
evidence: Observed in the current study.

claim: The proportion of mice with testicular microcalcifications increases to ~94% in hpg mice with concomitant global loss of the androgen receptor (hpg.ARKO).
source: The proportion of mice with testicular microcalcifications increased to ~94% in mice with concomitant global loss of the androgen receptor (AR) (hpg.ARKO) (O'Shaughnessy et al., 2009) (schematically illustrated in Figure 5A).
evidence: Observed in the current study and supported by citation to O'Shaughnessy et al., 2009.

claim: Sertoli cell-specific ablation of AR in hpg mice (hpg.SCARKO) does not augment the effect on microcalcifications in hpg mice.
source: Sertoli cell-specific ablation of AR in hpg mice (hpg.SCARKO) did not augment the effect on microcalcifications in the hpg mice, indicating a role of AR in peritubular cells (the only other cell type in the testis that express AR) or AR-expressing cells outside the testis for the formation of microcalcifications.
evidence: Observed in the current study.

claim: AR in peritubular cells or AR-expressing cells outside the testis may play a role in the formation of microcalcifications.
source: Sertoli cell-specific ablation of AR in hpg mice (hpg.SCARKO) did not augment the effect on microcalcifications in the hpg mice, indicating a role of AR in peritubular cells (the only other cell type in the testis that express AR) or AR-expressing cells outside the testis for the formation of microcalcifications.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hpg.ARKO mice have more microcalcifications than hpg.SCARKO mice.

claim: Somatic cells are important for bone-like trans-differentiation in mice.
source: Thus, suggesting that somatic cells are important for the bone-like trans-differentiation in mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observations in hpg, hpg.SCARKO, and hpg.ARKO mice showing that AR status affects microcalcification frequency.

claim: hpg, hpg.SCARKO, and hpg.ARKO mice have higher expression of Slc34a1 compared with WT mice.
source: Noteworthy, a shift in the expression of phosphate transporters was observed in the testis of hpg, hpg.SCARKO, and hpg.ARKO mice which had higher expression of Slc34a1 and lower expression of Slc20a1 and Slc34a2 compared with WT mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: hpg, hpg.SCARKO, and hpg.ARKO mice have lower expression of Slc20a1 and Slc34a2 compared with WT mice.
source: Noteworthy, a shift in the expression of phosphate transporters was observed in the testis of hpg, hpg.SCARKO, and hpg.ARKO mice which had higher expression of Slc34a1 and lower expression of Slc20a1 and Slc34a2 compared with WT mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: Bglap is detected in testis from all hpg.ARKO and most hpg.SCARKO mice.
source: However, Bglap was detected in testis from all hpg.ARKO and most hpg.SCARKO mice, suggesting that Bglap is expressed in mice with disturbed Sertoli cell maturation with the highest expression found in hpg.ARKO mice which had a 94% prevalence of microcalcifications (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: Bglap is expressed in mice with disturbed Sertoli cell maturation.
source: However, Bglap was detected in testis from all hpg.ARKO and most hpg.SCARKO mice, suggesting that Bglap is expressed in mice with disturbed Sertoli cell maturation with the highest expression found in hpg.ARKO mice which had a 94% prevalence of microcalcifications (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Bglap is detected in hpg.ARKO and hpg.SCARKO mice which have disturbed Sertoli cell maturation.

claim: Ablation of Sertoli cells at postnatal day 18 induces substantial microcalcifications in adult mice (80 days of age).
source: Ablation of Sertoli cells at postnatal day 18 induced substantial microcalcifications in the adult mice (80 days of age) as shown by alizarin red and von Kossa staining (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red and von Kossa staining in Sertoli cell-ablated mice in the current study.

claim: Microcalcifications induced by Sertoli cell ablation at postnatal day 18 persist when assessed in mice 1 year of age.
source: The microcalcifications persisted when assessed in mice 1 year of age (data not shown).
evidence: Observed in the current study.

claim: The timing of Sertoli cell ablation is important for microcalcification formation.
source: The timing of ablation seemed important because Sertoli cell ablation in adulthood (after puberty) did not cause microcalcifications when evaluated after 90 days but was detectable 1 year later (data not shown).
evidence: Observed in the current study.

claim: Sertoli cell ablation in adulthood does not cause microcalcifications when evaluated after 90 days but is detectable 1 year later.
source: The timing of ablation seemed important because Sertoli cell ablation in adulthood (after puberty) did not cause microcalcifications when evaluated after 90 days but was detectable 1 year later (data not shown).
evidence: Observed in the current study.

claim: Immature prepubertal cells are more prone to form microcalcifications.
source: This shows that immature prepubertal cells are more prone to form microcalcifications.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sertoli cell ablation before puberty causes rapid microcalcification formation while ablation in adulthood takes much longer.

claim: The formation of microcalcifications depends on the presence of germ cells with stem cell potential.
source: The formation of microcalcifications depends on the presence of germ cells with stem cell potential as ablation of Sertoli cells during embryonic development, which causes loss of germ cells, did not result in testicular microcalcifications.
evidence: Demonstrated by the observation that embryonic Sertoli cell ablation (which causes germ cell loss) does not result in microcalcifications in the current study.

claim: Ablation of Sertoli cells during embryonic development causes loss of germ cells and does not result in testicular microcalcifications.
source: The formation of microcalcifications depends on the presence of germ cells with stem cell potential as ablation of Sertoli cells during embryonic development, which causes loss of germ cells, did not result in testicular microcalcifications.
evidence: Observed in the current study.

claim: ALP activity is markedly higher in GCNIS tubules compared with normal seminiferous tubules.
source: ALP activity was markedly higher in GCNIS tubules compared with normal seminiferous tubules as determined by NBT/BCIP staining (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by NBT/BCIP staining in the current study.

claim: All four types of ALPs are expressed in normal testis.
source: All four types of ALPs were expressed in normal testis and the expression in GCNIS with microlithiasis and seminoma was not significantly higher, although some tumor specimens have marked expression of all four ALP isozymes.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: The expression of ALPs in GCNIS with microlithiasis and seminoma is not significantly higher than in normal testis.
source: All four types of ALPs were expressed in normal testis and the expression in GCNIS with microlithiasis and seminoma was not significantly higher, although some tumor specimens have marked expression of all four ALP isozymes.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR and statistical analysis in the current study.

claim: Some tumor specimens have marked expression of all four ALP isozymes.
source: All four types of ALPs were expressed in normal testis and the expression in GCNIS with microlithiasis and seminoma was not significantly higher, although some tumor specimens have marked expression of all four ALP isozymes.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: ALP activity in GCNIS/TGCTs is typically mediated by a combination of different isozymes rather than a single type of ALP.
source: This shows that ALP activity is higher in GCNIS/TGCTs and typically mediated by a combination of different isozymes rather than a single type of ALP (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all four ALP isozymes are expressed in tumor specimens.

claim: Mineralization is observed in GC1 cells after co-treatment with calcium and phosphate for 2 days.
source: Mineralization was already observed after co-treatment with calcium and phosphate for 2 days, but also after 7 days of treatment with calcium or phosphate alone (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: Mineralization is observed in GC1 cells after 7 days of treatment with calcium or phosphate alone.
source: Mineralization was already observed after co-treatment with calcium and phosphate for 2 days, but also after 7 days of treatment with calcium or phosphate alone (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: With low serum phosphate concentration (0.9 mM), 3 mM calcium is required to obtain rapid mineralization after 2 days in GC1 cells.
source: With a low serum phosphate concentration (0.9 mM), 3 mM calcium was required to obtain rapid mineralization after 2 days, whereas even 4 mM phosphate did not induce mineralization in a normal calcium concentration (1.8 mM) after 2 or 4 days.
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: 4 mM phosphate does not induce mineralization in GC1 cells at normal calcium concentration (1.8 mM) after 2 or 4 days.
source: With a low serum phosphate concentration (0.9 mM), 3 mM calcium was required to obtain rapid mineralization after 2 days, whereas even 4 mM phosphate did not induce mineralization in a normal calcium concentration (1.8 mM) after 2 or 4 days.
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: An increment in calcium to 2.0 mM enables five of six phosphate doses to induce rapid mineralization of GC1 cells.
source: However, an increment in calcium to 2.0 mM enabled five of the six phosphate doses to induce rapid mineralization of the GC1 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: Low calcium levels are protective in the high intratesticular phosphate environment.
source: This shows that low calcium levels are protective in the high intratesticular phosphate environment.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mineralization requires higher calcium concentrations even with high phosphate.

claim: Longer exposure to calcium and phosphate (4 and 7 days) augments the mineralization response in GC1 cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Longer exposure (4 and 7 days) augmented the response in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: The addition of PPi reduces mineralization in GC1 cells.
source: The addition of PPi, an inhibitor of mineralization, reduced mineralization, whereas co-treatment with PPi and pyrophosphatase (PPA1) that catalyzes the hydrolysis of PPi to inorganic phosphate (Pi) reintroduced mineralization (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: Co-treatment with PPi and pyrophosphatase (PPA1) reintroduces mineralization in GC1 cells.
source: The addition of PPi, an inhibitor of mineralization, reduced mineralization, whereas co-treatment with PPi and pyrophosphatase (PPA1) that catalyzes the hydrolysis of PPi to inorganic phosphate (Pi) reintroduced mineralization (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: TCam2 cells have high ALP activity as assessed by NBT/BCIP staining.
source: To assess the regulation of phosphatase activity in germ cells, a human cell line TCam2 was used as a positive control. TCam2 is derived from a seminoma and retains high expression of ectopic ALP, as assessed by NBT/BCIP staining, which was critically dependent on an alkaline environment with marked phosphatase activity at pH 9, but not at pH 7 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Demonstrated by NBT/BCIP staining in TCam2 cells in the current study.

claim: ALP activity in TCam2 cells is critically dependent on an alkaline environment with marked phosphatase activity at pH 9, but not at pH 7.
source: To assess the regulation of phosphatase activity in germ cells, a human cell line TCam2 was used as a positive control. TCam2 is derived from a seminoma and retains high expression of ectopic ALP, as assessed by NBT/BCIP staining, which was critically dependent on an alkaline environment with marked phosphatase activity at pH 9, but not at pH 7 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Demonstrated by NBT/BCIP staining at different pH in TCam2 cells in the current study.

claim: ALP activity is increased in GC1 cells in the presence of osteogenic medium compared with control medium.
source: Staining with Fast Blue RR revealed that ALP activity was increased in the presence of osteogenic medium compared with control medium, indicating that germ cells increase their ALP activity in the presence of factors that facilitate bone differentiation (Figure 6F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Fast Blue RR staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: Germ cells increase their ALP activity in the presence of factors that facilitate bone differentiation.
source: Staining with Fast Blue RR revealed that ALP activity was increased in the presence of osteogenic medium compared with control medium, indicating that germ cells increase their ALP activity in the presence of factors that facilitate bone differentiation (Figure 6F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that osteogenic medium increases ALP activity in GC1 cells.

claim: Wild-type mouse testicles cultured for 14 days with osteogenic medium -/+ phosphate do not change the expression of Bglap, Runx2, or Alpl.
source: However, an ex vivo model using wild-type mouse testicles (Figure 7A) cultured for 14 days with osteogenic medium -/+ phosphate did not change the expression of the bone markers Bglap, Runx2, or Alpl (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in mouse testis ex vivo cultures in the current study.

claim: Focal expression of RUNX2 is observed more often in mouse testis specimens treated with osteogenic medium than in specimens treated with vehicle.
source: However, occasionally one or few tubules had expression of RUNX2, which was observed more often in specimens treated with osteogenic medium than in specimens treated with vehicle (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in mouse testis ex vivo cultures in the current study.

claim: RUNX2 expression is switched to the bone-specific isoform during ex vivo culturing of mouse testis.
source: This suggests that RUNX2 expression was switched to the bone-specific isoform (Kanto et al., 2016) during ex vivo culturing and in accordance RUNX2 was more frequently found in specimens treated with the osteogenic cocktail+high phosphate.
evidence: Inferred from the detection of RUNX2 using an antibody targeting exon 5 (bone-specific isoform) in ex vivo cultures, and supported by citation to Kanto et al., 2016.

claim: PPi prevents mineralization induced by calcium and phosphate in the GC1 cell line.
source: One of the most potent mineralization inhibitors is PPi, which can be degraded by ALP or pyrophosphatase (Orriss, 2020). PPi prevented the mineralization induced by calcium and phosphate in the GC1 cell line, which was reintroduced in the presence of pyrophosphatase-degrading PPi.
evidence: Demonstrated by alizarin red staining in GC1 cells in the current study.

claim: PPi is a potent inhibitor of spermatogonial mineralization.
source: This highlights the role of PPi as an inhibitor of spermatogonial mineralization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PPi prevents mineralization in GC1 cells.

claim: ALPs are expressed by primordial and malignant germ cells.
source: ALPs convert PPi to Pi and are expressed by primordial and malignant germ cells (Hofmann et al., 1989; Jacobsen and Nørgaard‐pedersen, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hofmann et al., 1989; Jacobsen and Nørgaard‐pedersen, 1984).

claim: All four genes encoding ALPs in humans are expressed in malignant germ cells.
source: Four genes encode ALPs in humans (five in mice), and all are expressed in malignant germ cells, including the tissue nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP) (Hofmann et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hofmann et al., 1989 and demonstrated by qRT-PCR in the current study.

claim: TNAP is required for normal bone formation.
source: TNAP is required for normal bone formation and regulates vascular matrix mineralization by inactivation of the mineralization inhibitors PPi and OPN (Lomashvili et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lomashvili et al., 2004.

claim: TNAP regulates vascular matrix mineralization by inactivation of PPi and OPN.
source: TNAP is required for normal bone formation and regulates vascular matrix mineralization by inactivation of the mineralization inhibitors PPi and OPN (Lomashvili et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lomashvili et al., 2004.

claim: TCam2 cells have high ALP activity in alkaline pH.
source: We show here that TCam2 cells have high ALP activity in alkaline pH, suggesting that mineralization is promoted by malignant cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by NBT/BCIP staining in the current study.

claim: Mineralization is promoted by malignant cells.
source: We show here that TCam2 cells have high ALP activity in alkaline pH, suggesting that mineralization is promoted by malignant cells.
evidence: Inferred from the high ALP activity in TCam2 cells and the role of ALP in degrading mineralization inhibitors.

claim: Men with GCNIS and TGCTs are prone to microcalcifications due to lower PPi levels caused by increased ALP activity.
source: This implies that men with GCNIS and TGCTs are prone to microcalcifications due to lower PPi levels caused by increased ALP activity.
evidence: Inferred from the high ALP activity in GCNIS/TGCTs and the role of ALP in degrading PPi.

claim: The marked epididymal mineralization in Fgf23-/- mice occurs despite the presence of SIBLING proteins that inhibit hydroxyapatite formation.
source: Several other inhibitors and promoters of mineralization could be involved, but the marked epididymal mineralization observed in Fgf23-/- mice, despite the presence of SIBLING proteins that inhibit hydroxyapatite formation and the extensive testicular microcalcifications in men with loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2 (Corut et al., 2006), suggesting that aberrant function of just one component can be enough to promote the formation of microcalcifications.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC showing expression of OPN and DMP1 in Fgf23-/- mice with epididymal mineralization in the current study.

claim: Aberrant function of just one component can be enough to promote the formation of microcalcifications.
source: Several other inhibitors and promoters of mineralization could be involved, but the marked epididymal mineralization observed in Fgf23-/- mice, despite the presence of SIBLING proteins that inhibit hydroxyapatite formation and the extensive testicular microcalcifications in men with loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2 (Corut et al., 2006), suggesting that aberrant function of just one component can be enough to promote the formation of microcalcifications.
evidence: Inferred from observations in Fgf23-/- mice and patients with SLC34A2 loss-of-function variants.

claim: Immature bone formation in the testis is commonly observed in teratomas.
source: Immature bone formation in the testis is commonly observed in teratomas but can occur without malignancy.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mature bone tissue formation has been reported in the testis after trauma or bleeding without signs of GCNIS or invasive TGCTs.
source: Mature bone tissue formation has also been reported in the testis after trauma or bleeding without signs of GCNIS or invasive TGCTs (Yoneda et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoneda et al., 1979.

claim: Intratesticular bone was observed in a specimen despite no detection of GCNIS or malignant cells.
source: Here, we also show intratesticular bone in a specimen despite no detection of GCNIS or malignant cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by histological examination in the current study.

claim: Germ cells adjacent to intratesticular bone tissue have focally bone-specific RUNX2 positive cells but none express other investigated bone markers or show deposition of hydroxyapatite.
source: A comprehensive analysis of germ cells adjacent to the bone tissue revealed focally bone-specific RUNX2 positive germ cells but none of them expressed the other investigated bone markers or deposition of hydroxyapatite, indicating that the mature bone has been formed in the interstitial compartment through a different mechanism related to the trauma rather than alterations in mineral homeostasis leading to testicular microcalcifications.
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC staining in the current study.

claim: Mature bone adjacent to testicular tissue has been formed in the interstitial compartment through a mechanism related to trauma rather than alterations in mineral homeostasis.
source: A comprehensive analysis of germ cells adjacent to the bone tissue revealed focally bone-specific RUNX2 positive germ cells but none of them expressed the other investigated bone markers or deposition of hydroxyapatite, indicating that the mature bone has been formed in the interstitial compartment through a different mechanism related to the trauma rather than alterations in mineral homeostasis leading to testicular microcalcifications.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of bone markers in germ cells and the absence of microcalcifications in the testicular tissue.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications occur due to either malignant or benign etiology.
source: In conclusion, we show that the formation of testicular microcalcifications occurs due to either malignant or benign etiology, and includes one or more of the following events: aberrant function of Sertoli cells, disturbed local phosphate homeostasis, change in mineralization inhibitors, or aberrant germ cell function.
evidence: Demonstrated by observations in both human specimens with TGCTs and various mouse models with benign microcalcifications in the current study.

claim: Microcalcifications alone should not be considered a marker for malignancy in the testis.
source: Thus, this study suggests that microcalcifications alone should not be considered a marker for malignancy in the testis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that microcalcifications occur in both malignant and benign conditions.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications, both benign and malignant, occur secondary to changes in gonadal phosphate homeostasis.
source: This translational study demonstrates that testicular microcalcifications, both benign and malignant, occur secondary to changes in gonadal phosphate homeostasis and are often accompanied by a subsequent osteogenic-like differentiation of germ cells or testicular somatic cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by altered expression of phosphate transporters in human and mouse specimens with microcalcifications in the current study.

claim: Testicular microcalcifications are often accompanied by osteogenic-like differentiation of germ cells or testicular somatic cells.
source: This translational study demonstrates that testicular microcalcifications, both benign and malignant, occur secondary to changes in gonadal phosphate homeostasis and are often accompanied by a subsequent osteogenic-like differentiation of germ cells or testicular somatic cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by expression of bone markers (Osteocalcin, RUNX2, DMP1, OPN) in cells adjacent to microcalcifications in the current study.

claim: Microcalcifications are more prevalent in testicular biopsies with GCNIS than without.
source: Microcalcifications are more prevalent in testicular biopsies with GCNIS than without (Kang et al., 1994), which highlights that GCNIS or TGCTs release factors involved in the development of microlithiasis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kang et al., 1994.

claim: GCNIS or TGCTs release factors involved in the development of microlithiasis.
source: Microcalcifications are more prevalent in testicular biopsies with GCNIS than without (Kang et al., 1994), which highlights that GCNIS or TGCTs release factors involved in the development of microlithiasis.
evidence: Inferred from the higher prevalence of microcalcifications in GCNIS-containing biopsies and supported by observations in NTera2 xenograft mice.

claim: Impaired Sertoli cell function appears to be of greater importance than the presence of malignant germ cells for the formation of microcalcifications.
source: Still, the accompanied impaired Sertoli cell function appears to be of greater importance than the presence of malignant germ cells.
evidence: Inferred from observations in hpg, hpg.SCARKO, hpg.ARKO mice, and Sertoli cell-ablated mice showing that Sertoli cell dysfunction is associated with microcalcifications.

claim: Impaired Sertoli cell function in both mice and humans increases the risk of testicular microlithiasis.
source: In this manuscript, we show that impaired Sertoli cell function in both mice and humans increases the risk of testicular microlithiasis and this association seems to be more persistent than the malignant linkage.
evidence: Demonstrated by observations in Sertoli cell-ablated mice, hpg mice, and human specimens with Sertoli cell dysfunction in the current study.

claim: FGF23 is highly expressed in GCNIS, EC, and hESC but not in classical seminoma.
source: The systemic master regulator of phosphate, FGF23, is highly expressed in GCNIS, EC, and hESC but not in classical seminoma.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR, IHC, and Western blot in the current study.

claim: The expression of FGF23 is linked with the transformation of GCNIS to invasive EC.
source: This suggests that the expression of FGF23 is linked with the transformation of GCNIS to the invasive EC and is not a result of duplication of chromosome 12p which is also prevalent in classical seminoma.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FGF23 is expressed in GCNIS and EC but not in seminoma, despite both EC and seminoma having chromosome 12p duplication.

claim: FGF23 expression is not a result of duplication of chromosome 12p.
source: This suggests that the expression of FGF23 is linked with the transformation of GCNIS to the invasive EC and is not a result of duplication of chromosome 12p which is also prevalent in classical seminoma.
